title: Williams reveal special livery ahead of Spanish GP in Madrid
excerpt:
Williams will mark Formula 1's return to Madrid by racing a special edition livery inspired by the colours of their 1981 championship-winning FW07C, which was the car the team raced the last time the sport competed in the Spanish capital.

The livery, which will adorn the cars of home hero Carlos Sainz and his team mate Alex Albon, features a white, green and navy blue colourway in a nod to the 1981-design that was raced by Alan Jones and Carlos Reutemann at Madrid's Circuito de Jarama.

Williams say the design showcases how they are using the knowledge, methods and lessons of the past to inspire their fight back to the front.

"From the engineers who developed the FW07C to the team mates preparing the FW48, the same spirit of innovation, precision and teamwork continues to shape Williams," said the British team.

The one-off design was revealed during a Fan Zone appearance with Sainz in Madrid's Plaza De Callao on Tuesday evening, ahead of the first Spanish Grand Prix on the new part-street, part-purpose-built 22-turn Madring.

“Our mission to get back to the front of the grid is drawn from, inspired by and informed by everything we’ve done before," said Team Principal James Vowles.

"I am incredibly proud to celebrate that through [title sponsor] Atlassian’s special livery, connecting the team we were at Jarama with the team we are becoming today through focused collaboration, improved technological innovation, and real creativity.

"The car looks fantastic, and I cannot wait to see it lapping around Madrid.”

Sainz will be competing in his 13th Spanish Grand Prix but first in Madrid - the city where he was born, raised and began his motor racing career.

He and team mate Alex Albon will be searching for the team's first points since Albon took eighth in Monaco, eight Grand Prix weekends ago.

The British team, who finished a superb fifth last year, currently sit ninth in the Teams' Championship on 11 points, five adrift of Audi.

title: Why Antonelli’s Monza win feels like the defining moment of 2026
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli delivered what felt like a crowning moment on Sunday, winning his home race from 19th on the grid, in one of the great drives of recent years.

Arriving at Monza with a 59-point lead in the championship, but a grid penalty that would see him start at the back, this had to be the chance for his rivals to take a big chunk of points out of him. Instead, as Kimi ate pasta from his winner’s trophy on Sunday night, George Russell will be licking his wounds and realising that this season may well have just got away from him for good.

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Italy?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli claimed one of the great Formula 1 victories at the Italian Grand Prix last weekend. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges at Monza? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Having been consigned to P19 on the grid after power unit changes ahead of the weekend, Antonelli's goal in theory was focused on limiting the damage to his drivers' standings points lead. Instead, the Mercedes driver put in one of the all-time great drives to claim an unlikely victory in front of his home fans. Scything his way through the order, Antonelli was already battling team mate George Russell for the lead prior to the halfway point before heading to the pits under a Virtual Safety Car. With fresher tyres, Antonelli took chunks out of Russell while recovering positions, passing his title rival four laps from the end and becoming the first Italian to win their home race in 60 years after a drive for the ages. For that he scores a perfect 10 from our judges.

If Antonelli's victory on Sunday was the performance of the season, Pierre Gasly's Qualifying heroics the day before were not far behind. The Frenchman and Alpine used the Mercedes power unit to full effect and executed their flying laps perfectly, with Gasly topping both Q1 and the crucial Q3 session to claim his first F1 pole position. Staying there was always going to be an impossible task during the 53-lap race, and Gasly eventually slipped down to P7 but remained comfortably best of the rest at a venue where he scored his only F1 victory six years ago.

Despite lacking the straight-line speed of Mercedes drivers Antonelli and Russell, Max Verstappen certainly proved to be a thorn in their sides. The Red Bull driver moved from P5 into P2 during the early running before taking the lead and heading the pack for three laps. Eventually passed by both Russell and Antonelli, Verstappen initially stayed in touch, and like Antonelli made a stop under the VSC, before charging back up to P3 for his third podium in four races.

Arvid Lindblad once again went under the radar as the Racing Bulls driver finished a lonely P8 in Italy to claim more valuable points in the teams' standings. Lindblad had started ninth and benefitted from Charles Leclerc's crash, while Franco Colapinto's off-track moment at the Lesmos gifted the F1 rookie another spot. It means Lindblad has scored points seven times in the last eight races, ensuring Racing Bulls remain ahead of Alpine in the teams' standings.

Russell entered the weekend knowing it was a golden opportunity to start clawing back the 59-point deficit to Antonelli in the drivers' standings, with his team mate set to serve a grid penalty. Instead, the Briton left Monza seven points further back having not really put a foot wrong. The Mercedes man just missed out on pole position as his final flying lap was somewhat hampered by Verstappen, but Russell soon found himself in the lead of the race. Battery management and the power of the slipstream meant he was never able to pull away from Antonelli as the pair traded places in a brilliant battle. Fitted with the hard tyres also meant Russell was never seriously considered for a pit stop under the VSC like Antonelli on the medium. Despite his best efforts and a solid weekend performance, Russell once again lost out to Antonelli in arguably the most decisive hammer blow of the season.

After a difficult weekend in Zandvoort where he failed to match McLaren team mate and race winner Lando Norris, Oscar Piastri was back close to his best in Monza. The Australian took third on the grid, but blocking Liam Lawson in Q2 at the first chicane meant Piastri was hit with a three-place grid penalty. He soon began to make progress, though, and found himself in a tussle with Lewis Hamilton during the first half of the race for P4. Having got the better of the Ferrari driver, Piastri's attention in the final laps turned towards his team mate, with Norris just moving ahead on the final tour as the pair finished fourth and fifth.

After back-to-back wins, Norris was brought back to reality at Monza as McLaren failed to showcase race-winning form despite having a Mercedes power unit. Norris failed to string his final Qualifying lap together, which left the reigning World Champion only P8 on the grid, and meant he spent much of the race following others in the slipstream. After deposing Gasly and Hamilton, Norris battled fiercely with Piastri in the closing stages, eventually completing the move on the final lap on the run to the Ascari Chicane after a decent recovery drive.

It was a weekend of being so close yet so far for Gabriel Bortoleto and Audi. The Brazilian failed to reach the final part of Qualifying by just 0.001s, although Antonelli's grid drop meant Bortoleto did start inside the top 10 after all. In the race, the Audi driver didn't have quite enough pace to match the Racing Bulls and Alpines, with Bortoleto missing out on the points by seven seconds.

In just his second race back in F1 with Racing Bulls, Tsunoda reached the points in P10 having climbed up the order from P15 on the grid, potentially putting himself back in the driver market window for next season. The Japanese driver will get another run out in Madrid after Red Bull confirmed Liam Lawson would stay with the senior squad in place of the injured Isack Hadjar.

Despite having the Mercedes power unit, Williams always expected to struggle at Monza and so it proved. Even so, Carlos Sainz managed to battle his way to P13, beating Lawson's Red Bull and both upgraded Haas cars, finishing just 16 seconds away from the points after a solid drive.

Missing out

Just missing out on a top-10 place in our latest Power Rankings list are Franco Colapinto and Ollie Bearman. Colapinto managed to grab P9 for Alpine having run as high as third at one stage before going off the track, while Bearman utilised new upgrades on his Haas to finish P15.

title: Do Ferrari need to deliver some ‘home truths’ after Monza?
excerpt:
Ferrari’s Italian Grand Prix weekend was supposed to mark a step in the right direction as they unleashed more car upgrades and a new power unit – but their hopes of challenging for victory were undone by the exit of the first chicane.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton came perilously close to a major collision at the start of Sunday’s race, with the seven-time World Champion making a bold move down the inside of Turn 1, only to be pushed wide and into the gravel at the exit of Turn 2.

After the race, which he finished in a distant sixth position (Leclerc having retired via a heavy Lap 2 crash), Hamilton stated that Ferrari need to review “how we communicate” and ultimately “change things” when it comes to the two red cars going racing.

As the paddock packed down on Sunday evening, Davide Valsecchi and Lawrence Barretto teamed up to talk through the events in the latest episode of the F1 Nation podcast.

“We are speaking about the best driver in F1 history, or one of the best by result, and a huge talent that probably deserves a championship, and doesn’t have it yet,” said Valsecchi of Hamilton and Leclerc.

“How crazy is it? 400,000 people here watching for them, and they fight each other at the first corner. I’m sorry, I’m very disappointed about our drivers.”

Barretto added: “I’m disappointed that we didn’t get a chance to see what Ferrari’s pace really was around here in race trim because of that.

“If I take you back to the start of the weekend, I interviewed all three of them – Charles, Lewis and Fred [Vasseur, team boss] – in Milan, [at Ferrari’s] flagship store. They were so excited about the weekend, because they were bringing the engine upgrade, they brought some chassis updates specifically for Monza, which most teams weren’t really doing.

“I think there was this real belief that they’d been chipping away, and they could maybe make something magical happen at this magic track. It looked pretty good on Friday, and then Qualifying didn’t go their way, but suddenly with penalties that happened, they were third and fourth [on the grid].

“Charles’ view is probably that Lewis probably shouldn’t have stuck it up the inside at Turn 1. I’m not saying Charles did what he did deliberately to Lewis at Turn 2, but I think it's both of them [playing a part].

“In this moment, they defined the race already. It made no sense to go up against each other at Turn 1 and Turn 2, unless there is confusion between them as to how Ferrari are going to deal with this championship as we get into the spicy end.”

Barretto went on to argue that Ferrari must now seriously think about imposing rules of engagement – something Hamilton pushed during his post-race interviews.

“What is needed is for Lewis and Charles to sit down with Fred and go, ‘Right, this is what the rule is’,” he said. “One of them might not like it, but ‘this is what the rule is going forward’, because they are chasing Mercedes, who are up and away at the minute, and you can’t be throwing away potential results like this.

“Ferrari are very well positioned in that it’s Fred who’s going to have to have these chats, because I think it’s a very difficult conversation that he’s going have to have, with a seven-time World Champion and Ferrari’s golden child.

“It’s difficult, but fortunately for Fred, his man management has been incredible. That’s been one of his skillsets coming through the junior formulas and into F1, the way he manages drivers. He ran Charles at Sauber, Alfa Romeo, he’s brought him here, they can have a difficult conversation. Lewis, they’ve had this relationship for how many years now? They can have that difficult conversation.

“I think it is going to have to be them sat in a room, lock the door, get a bit of paper out, and have some hard truths. I’m not sure I would pick any team boss other than Fred, currently, to have that conversation. It’s got to be a tough conversation. They’ve got to have some home truths.”

Those incidents aside, Valsecchi thinks Monza has also shown that Ferrari are still too far away to put pressure on Mercedes in either championship battle – Hamilton trailing Kimi Antonelli by 76 points, and 122 points separating the two teams.

“We need to be realistic,” he commented. “We need to remember that after the fight [between the Ferraris], there was a red flag, and then a restart. Hamilton was immediately in the fight for taking the victory or a podium. He was eighth, Antonelli 12th, at the restart, and they [Ferrari] were not quick enough.

“The Mercedes engine scared the others, because today Mercedes were unbelievably strong. There was Alpine, there was [Lando] Norris, there was [Oscar] Piastri, and then there was Ferrari. So, if we want to be realistic, if we are going in the next few races where there are long straights, the Mercedes engine will have some advantage, and that is clear.”

title: What time is the 2026 Spanish GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The next round of the 2026 season sees the drivers take on something new - the Madring in Madrid, a brand new track where the pecking order will be a complete unknown.

Kimi Antonelli goes into the 14th race weekend with a healthy lead in the Drivers' Championship having won last time out at Monza, but Mercedes might not have it all their own way in Spain.

The Italian now leads team mate George Russell by 66 points, while Lewis Hamilton is a further 10 points adrift for Ferrari. But the form book may well be ripped up this weekend, with the Madring set to provide a stern test for driver and car alike.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix?

The weekend will begin with FP1 on Friday, 11 September, at 1330 local time, followed by FP2 at 1700.

A final hour of practice takes place at 1230 on Saturday, 12 September, before the drivers compete for the best grid spots in Qualifying at 1600. Lastly, the Grand Prix starts at 1500 on Sunday, 13 September.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix taking place?

The Spanish Grand Prix will be held at the Madring this year, with the track set to make its debut. Madrid has previously hosted F1 around 40 years ago at Jarama.

The track is easily accessible by public transport, being situated much closer to the centre of the city. It has a Miami-like feel, with a combination of public roads and private land making up the 22-corner circuit.

One of the many things to keep an eye on is the longest banked turn on the F1 calendar, while the looming walls mean the drivers will need to concentrate all race-long.

Spain hosts two Grands Prix this year, with Barcelona-Catalunya having already taken place, with Hamilton winning an emotional race for Ferrari.

What is the weather forecast in Spain?

Conditions are expected to be warm and sunny, with temperatures in excess of 30 Celsius across all three days of track action and minimal chance of rain in the region.

When can I watch F2 and F3 during the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix weekend?

Formula 2 returns to action this weekend, with Nikola Tsolov leading the Championship by 11 points from Rafael Camara.

Free Practice will start proceedings at 1105 local time on Friday, September 11, followed by Qualifying at 1500.

The Sprint Race, which sees the top 10 finishers from Qualifying reversed, will take place at 1415 on Saturday, September 12, before the lights go out for the Feature Race at 1125 on Sunday, September 13.

An F3 champion will be decided, with the series reaching its conclusion in Madrid.

Freddie Slater and Ugo Ugochukwu are set to battle for the title, with the former leading the standings by 15 points.

The weekend will begin with Free Practice at 0955 on Friday, September 11, with the field divided into two groups for Qualifying A at 1825 and Qualifying B at 1855.

The top 12 qualifiers will be reversed for the Sprint Race at 1105 on Saturday, September 12, with the first Feature Race the same day at 1800.

The second Feature Race will conclude the weekend and the season at 0945 on Sunday, September 13.

title: How Carlos Alcaraz’s bromance with Alonso made him an F1 fan
excerpt:
The Formula 1 paddock is no stranger to celebrity visitors, but few sporting stars have embraced it quite like Carlos Alcaraz. With the Spanish Grand Prix and US Open finals taking place this weekend, it's the perfect time to revisit the former World No. 1's links to F1, Grand Prix appearances to conversations with Fernando Alonso.

Tennis ace Carlos Alcaraz is back from injury, and will play in the US Open quarter-finals in New York later today, but he also has a close connection with the F1 paddock.

Although not a lifelong F1 fan, the 23-year-old is very loyal when it comes to his compatriots’ success on four wheels and is particularly inspired by Aston Martin’s Fernando Alonso.

How Carlos’ compatriot got him into F1

Carlos Alcaraz is very honest that he wasn’t previously a fan of F1 but, thanks to fellow Spaniard Alonso, he’s now much more engaged in the World Championship.

The first public confirmation of this sporting bromance came after Alcaraz’s victory at the 2023 Miami Open quarter-finals – a tournament held inside the Hard Rock Stadium, like the paddock for the Miami Grand Prix – where Alcaraz wrote ‘33? Soon’ on the broadcast camera. Many viewers were left confused at this vague message, but it was a direct call to Alonso ahead of that year’s Australian Grand Prix.

After two podiums at the start of the 2023 season – in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia – Alonso’s chances for a 33rd career win looked strong, and so the fun reference showed his support to the two-time World Champion.

Speaking about his love for Formula 1 to the media after the Miami match, Alcaraz said: “Fernando has made me into a Formula 1 fan. He’s made me watch races, made me support him. And what better way to support Fernando than with a message on the camera?”

He went on: “To me it’s crazy what he’s doing at his age. He’s basically in the fight for the Formula 1 World Championship.”

And he revealed that he had thought about what kind of F1 driver he would be: "I would be an aggressive one!”

The Murcia-born player also paid homage to Alonso's iconic celebration from the 2006 Japanese Grand Prix, where he put one leg up and stretched out both arms – a bit like the George Russell T-Pose, before it was a thing.

Carlos Alcaraz's tennis rival Jannik Sinner on his love for Formula 1

Visiting the paddock

After beginning his close friendship with Alonso, the next step was naturally getting the Spanish star to a Grand Prix despite his busy tennis schedule. Alcaraz and Matteo Berrettini were both able to enjoy the magic of the 2024 Italian Grand Prix after second-round exits at that year's US Open. Berrettini was also in attendance at Monza this year, where his fellow Italian Kimi Antonelli charged from 19th on the grid to claim a stunning victory.

Alcaraz was back again in 2026, visiting the F1 Paddock across the Bahrain pre-season testing as he was in the area for a tournament. From there he spent time in a variety of garages, including McLaren, Aston Martin, Williams and Ferrari, filming content with his countrymen.

Carlos², as it was affectionately described by Williams, saw Alcaraz catch up with Carlos Sainz over the testing day, but rather than chat about cars or tennis the subject naturally gravitated to...yep, you guessed it: golf.

It was then time to visit the Aston Martin garage, and plenty of hugs were shared between Alcaraz and his hero Alonso, before a garage tour and a chance to listen into the team radio.

There are also photos of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc with the tennis star in the Scuderia Ferrari hub.

From Grand Slam success to football fandom – How F1 has become sport’s ultimate crossover

F1’s obsession with tennis

Current World Number 1 Jannik Sinner – who is currently out of play with injury – was present at last weekend’s Italian Grand Prix, and is known to be a close friend of drivers’ standings leader Antonelli, with the two both being Italian sporting stars. Sinner became a Friend of F1 in 2023, and has been present at several events over the past few seasons, even waving the chequered flag for the Abu Dhabi season finale in 2024.

Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, Serena Williams and Berrettini have all been spotted in the Formula 1 paddock this season, but the fixation between tennis and F1 works both ways. The ball has been in the other court – literally – when drivers have been courtside watching tennis tournaments.

During a break in races earlier this year, several of the grid made the trip to the Monte Carlo Masters to watch some excellent tennis up close. In one day, Gabriel Bortoleto, Oliver Bearman, Oscar Piastri and Alexander Albon all posed for a photograph with Sinner, later watching from courtside, with Leclerc and Russell also attending matches during the clay tournament.

Plenty of the grid also headed to Wimbledon this summer, with Russell, Bearman and Liam Lawson all in attendance, as well as Antonelli who watched from the Royal Box alongside tennis legend Roger Federer.

title: Vettel reflects on driving Schumacher's 2002 Ferrari
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel admits that getting behind the wheel of his idol and friend Michael Schumacher's Ferrari F2002 ahead of last weekend's Italian Grand Prix was "a very emotional moment".

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, with the German taking victory in the 1996 Italian GP as he embarked on an 11-year spell with Ferrari which yielded five drivers' and six teams' titles.

After returning to Formula 1 following semi-retirement, Schumacher retired from the sport in 2012 after three years with Mercedes.

Vettel, who grew up with Schumacher as his boyhood hero before becoming friends with the seven-time World Champion during his own F1 career, was on hand at Monza to drive Schumacher's F2002.

The car helped Schumacher to clinch his third title with Ferrari in 2002 during a campaign where the German finished on the podium in all 17 races, a feat still unmatched.

"First and foremost, it's for my friend and to remember that, which was a very emotional moment," said Vettel when asked about the experience ahead of driving the F2002.

"He's my childhood hero and later on we had a deep connection with the friendship and got fairly close and shared so many nice memories. I think we'd much rather see him drive today than me, myself included.

"I'm looking forward to the moment in the car because I think it will be a moment where we will feel Michael and what he stands for still and hear him.

"I think there's so much more than just a couple of laps. It's his car, but it's a championship-winning car. It's a Ferrari. In Monza, around Tifosi.

"I think that there's a lot more in there that makes a connection to me. I mean, I love the sport. I don't race anymore, but I still love it, and I probably will love racing as long as I live. That's why I believe I care so much, and these moments are so special."

Schumacher's former team mate Rubens Barrichello was also on hand over the weekend and drove the F2002 on Saturday, while Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton used a special livery inspired by Schumacher.

title: The biggest recovery drives to win in F1
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli added his name to the list of Formula 1 race winners who have surged from a lowly grid position to claim victory, doing so in stunning style on home turf at the Italian Grand Prix.

We take a look back at the other drivers who have found themselves staring at a swathe of rear wings on the starting grid only to wind up greeting the chequered flag before anyone else...

8. Michael Schumacher (1995 Belgian Grand Prix, 16th)

Michael Schumacher won 91 Grands Prix during his distinguished career, but none from lower than 16th on the grid. Schumacher made progress through the pack at Spa-Francorchamps in 1995, during which phase early leader David Coulthard retired, and a slick tyre gamble when it rained proved influential.

Schumacher moved into the lead, which he brilliantly defended against an increasingly frustrated wet-shod rival Damon Hill, despite his inferior tyre situation. The Williams eventually got through – only to make a mistake, before returning to the pit lane for slicks on a drying track.

However, it proved ill-timed, as the rain returned and intensified. Both Schumacher and Hill took on wet tyres, but any challenge from Hill dissipated due to a penalty for pit lane speeding, giving Schumacher a clear run to victory.

7. Kimi Raikkonen (2005 Japanese Grand Prix, 17th)

Qualifying took part in changeable weather at Suzuka, and in an era of one-shot qualifying drivers encountered varying track conditions. It left most of the usual front-runners at the back of the grid, including newly-crowned champion Fernando Alonso in 16th, and Kimi Raikkonen in 17th.

In a frenetic race, featuring some spectacular wheel-to-wheel racing, Raikkonen and Alonso carved their way through the pack, and it was the McLaren ace who fronted the challenge. A late stop to refuel put Raikkonen on the coattails of Alonso’s Renault team-mate Giancarlo Fisichella, and he caught the Italian in the closing laps.

As the pair began the final lap Raikkonen seized the outside line and brilliantly swept around Fisichella to take the lead, and with it, pull off a remarkable comeback victory.

6. Max Verstappen (2024 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, 17th)

Having won seven of the opening 10 rounds in 2024, Max Verstappen then went on a 10-race winless spell, during which phase his title advantage was gradually reduced by Lando Norris.

Qualifying in Sao Paulo was postponed from Saturday to early Sunday morning on account of weather, and in a disrupted session Verstappen was caught out, qualifying 12th, and he started 17th on the grid due to a power unit penalty – though this was a net 15th due to two cars ahead not starting.

From there, Verstappen put on a masterclass in tricky conditions, moving through the pack, before making further gains when the red flag was shown mid-race – allowing him to change wet tyres. Verstappen still trailed Esteban Ocon, but after a handful of laps overhauled the Alpine driver, and went on to triumph by almost 20 seconds. It was a drive that all but sealed a fourth straight crown for the imperious Verstappen.

Remembering Verstappen's era-defining win in Sao Paulo

5. John Watson, (1982 Detroit Grand Prix, 17th)

John Watson qualified only 17th on the grid for Formula 1’s first visit to the streets of Detroit, during a weekend that was laced by organisational issues and tricky conditions.

Watson opted for the harder tyres for the race and it proved to be a tactical masterstroke, as he passed rivals with aplomb, including a stunning trio of passes on a single lap – including on team mate Niki Lauda.

Watson quickly reeled in and passed an ailing Keke Rosberg, before pulling away and taking a relatively comfortable win. Remarkably, of his five Grand Prix victories, Watson claimed another win from even further down the starting grid…

4. Rubens Barrichello (2000 German Grand Prix, 18th)

A messy qualifying session left Rubens Barrichello down in 18th position and out-of-place, and he quickly made amends by undertaking a sequence of overtakes in the early laps, blasting his Ferrari past rivals along the hefty full-throttle sections of the old Hockenheim.

A Safety Car for a man entering the circuit bunched the field, and a communication mix-up cost McLaren, elevating Barrichello to second behind only Mika Hakkinen. When rain swept across the circuit Hakkinen stopped for wets, but Barrichello stuck it out on slicks, and with the large venue only partially dampened there were sufficient dry parts to ensure Barrichello was not threatened.

Not only did Barrichello complete a remarkable comeback win, but it was also his maiden victory after seven years in the sport.

3. Bill Vukovich (1954 Indianapolis 500, 19th)

Back in the 1950s the Indianapolis 500 was part of the World Championship, but very few Formula 1 drivers or teams ever ventured to the Speedway, nor did the oval racers contest other Grands Prix – meaning that forever a smattering of Indy 500s remain something of an anomalous outlier.

Bill Vukovich was one such example, and he contested the Indy 500 on five occasions in the 1950s, winning the prestigious event in 1953 and 1954. For the second of those successes Vukovich started only 19th but worked his way forwards to triumph, though that remains shy of the Brickyard’s record, with the event having twice been won from 28th.

Vukovich died at the following year’s race after being involved in an accident while leading.

2. Kimi Antonelli (2026 Italian Grand Prix, 19th)

Reliability problems earlier in 2026 meant Kimi Antonelli was on the trajectory towards receiving a grid penalty for taking on fresh power unit components, and Mercedes duly removed emotion from the equation by taking the hit at Monza.

Antonelli started 19th, after Liam Lawson and Fernando Alonso opted for pit lane starts, and was 12th when the race was suspended for Charles Leclerc’s accident. Antonelli vaulted to eighth at the restart and swiftly picked off rivals, going on to exchange top spot with team-mate George Russell.

A pit stop mid-race left Antonelli playing catch-up once more, but with strong pace and fresher tyres he worked his way up back to the top, surviving a late scare courtesy of a mistake exiting the first chicane to take the lead and the win.

1. John Watson (1983 US Grand Prix West, 22nd)

McLaren was a contender in 1983 but on one-lap pace the team struggled to find a balance at bumpy Long Beach, leaving John Watson and Niki Lauda 22nd and 23rd respectively on the grid, four seconds off pole position.

They were also hampered by the poor ability of their qualifying tyres, but in race trim, the two cars flew. In an attritional race both Watson and Lauda sliced their way through the pack, making moves while gaining from their opponents encountering setbacks.

Such was the speed of the McLaren in race trim that Watson won from Lauda by almost half a minute, with only Ferrari’s Rene Arnoux – over a minute behind – still on the lead lap.

title: Carlos Sainz addresses Madrid F1 concern after red flag chaos
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has played down the disruption F1 sessions could endure at Madrid next weekend.

The Madring will make its F1 debut when it hosts round 14 of the 2026 season, taking over as the location of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The track has been under construction for several years and recently held an in-season Formula 3 test in anticipation of the maiden race event.

During the test, 19 red flags were deployed across two days, 11 of which were for contact with the barrier.

It has generated concern that it could mean chaos for F1 this weekend, with Sainz acknowledging that the track will be a major challenge.

“With the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track, it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in F1 recently,” he said.

“The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways.

“So having that in F1 with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge.”

However, Sainz insisted that F1 is no stranger to dealing with the challenge of high-speed street tracks with close barriers.

As a result, he does not expect the weekend to to feature many chaotic incidents.

“Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars and red flags and yellow flags in quali.

“But it's been a fashion or a tendency of F1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah or Baku that are closer to the city.

“They have more walls, and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well at every place we've gone.

“It's that same similar trend that we're going towards.”

title: Sebastian Vettel addresses losing F1 youngest champion record to Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel says he would be "very happy" to lose his tag as the 'youngest F1 world champion' to runaway 2026 leader Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli leads the points table by 66 points following his Italian GP success last time out, coming through from 19th on the grid to claim a historic victory, his seventh of the season.

With potential 10 races remaining, Antonelli holds a buffer of nearly three grands prix worth over George Russell, and a further buffer of seven wins to Russell's two in case countback is required to seperate the two.

Having just turned 20 years old, Antonelli is on course to shatter Vettel's record from 2010 by over three years, with the German, who was born on July 3rd, 1987, having won his first title on November 14th, 2010 - at the age of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days.

For Antonelli to beat that, the Italian, who was born on August 25th, 2006, must win the F1 title before Saturday, 5th January 2030.

If the 2026 season goes down to the final race, currently scheduled for December 6th in Abu Dhabi, but understood to be moving to Europe, Antonelli would be 20 years, 3 months, 12 days.

Addressing the prospect of losing the record he's held for 16 years, Vettel was sanguine about the possibility.

"No," Vettel told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if it would be bittersweet to lose his record to Antonelli.

"I'd be very happy for him. He's had an incredible year, and there's the old phrase that records are there to be broken.

"He still has a lot of years ahead of him to do so.

"I love the sport, so as a spectator, it's very exciting. I'd wish for the others to come back and be more in the mix, but I'm sort of independent and happy for them because I know how much work there is behind it to achieve it.

"And whoever will win will deserve it."

title: George Russell details F1 title approach after latest setback
excerpt:
George Russell has conceded it will be “exceptionally challenging” to overcome Kimi Antonelli's advantage in the drivers' championship this year.

As a result, the Briton insisted he is giving no thought to the title fight.

Russell entered the Italian Grand Prix last weekend with a strong opportunity to eat into Antonelli's lead as the local favourite took a grid penalty for a new engine.

However, Antonelli quickly worked his way through the pack and soon found himself in the fight for the lead against Russell, passing him in the closing stages on fresher tyres.

Antonelli's victory now puts him 66 points ahead of Russell, leading the latter to praise his team-mate.

“Definitely Kimi’s in control of it and he’s deserving to be in control of it,” Russell told media including RacingNews365.

“For me personally, I’m not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything.

“I’m just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend.”

Antonelli has had the upper hand on Russell for much of the year and has consistently edged out the gap as he targets a maiden title.

Russell asserted his target going forward is simply to maximise race weekends, rather than focusing on the points difference.

“He’s performing incredibly well,” Russell added. “It’s going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap.

“I’m just sort of accepting that it is what it is and I’m just going to enjoy it from here on in and try and win as many races as possible.”

title: Formula E reveal crucial agreement in major global partnership
excerpt:
Formula E CEO Jeff Dodds has confirmed that there are agreements in place for Disney+ to advertise Formula E, following last month's announcement that it will become the official global streaming partner of the championship.

It was announced in August that, as part of a multi-year agreement, Formula E will be available on Disney+ across 144 territories, including the UK and the USA.

As part of the deal, every practice session, qualifying session and race will be available live, as will preview and review shows, highlights, on-demand replays and behind-the-scenes content.

It is one of, if not the biggest and most significant partnerships in the history of the all-electric series, and one which, with the exciting arrival of Gen4, should result in a substantial increase in global viewership.

Crucially, Disney+ will also advertise the series, something Amazon Prime failed to do for Formula E's 'Driver' docuseries. While the docuseries, which ran for two seasons, was impressive, it was practically impossible to find on the streaming site.

Finding it was only possible by specifically searching for 'Driver', creating an unwanted barrier to attracting new fans. Based on the agreements in place with Disney+, the same should be avoided.

Dodds is more than aware that Formula E will not be front and centre all the time on the platform, especially with significant movie releases coming up for Disney, but he has expressed that the American company is invested in and eager to grow the series.

"So yes, there are agreements with Disney about how they'll promote the racing," Dodds told RacingNews365 during an interview. "The difference being [from Amazon], this is an early sport for Disney+, and they have a very strong vested interest in this being really successful for them.

"They're investing a lot of resources into this, so I think we're mutually aligned that as you move into a race weekend, it's going to have prominence. People are going to know there's a race going on, and they're going to be directed, navigated through the platform to find it.

"On the other hand, they have a lot of new releases, right? So they'll be releasing big Marvel releases and things like that. It would be naive to think we're always going to be the most important thing on that platform because they have a lot of really important things on that platform.

"But yeah, we've talked to them about the promotion of the race series being really important to us, and they've given us all the reassurances we need that they will absolutely land that for us."

title: F1 braced for 'most severe' test with high-stress La Monumental Madring corner
excerpt:
Pirelli's chief F1 tyre engineer believes the championship will face the "most severe turn" with the "critical" banking at the new La Monumental corner at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Turn 12 at the new Madring is a long banked right-hander corner, which whilst not as steep in gradient as the final corner at Zandvoort, is considerably longer and will be taken at higher speed.

La Monumental has around 13.5 degrees of bank, far lower than Zandvoort, or indeed AVUS in Germany, which had a remarkable 43 degrees of bank.

This will place more stress on the tyres owing to the lateral loads, with Pirelli bringing the C2-C3-C4 tyres to the new race in the Spanish capital.

Whilst it does have some real-life track data from Ferrari's demo outing earlier in the year and the FIA F3 test, which featured 19 red flags over two days, Simone Berra believes the F1 drivers will be limited by pure grip available and not limited by power around the "critical and severe" banking.

"We gathered a lot of information, we went there also to measure the track because obviously it's very important to characterise as well the tarmac, which is an important factor for the tyres," Berra told media, including RacingNews365.

"The tarmac is pretty smooth as usual for a new tarmac. I would say also the level of bitumen is quite high, as they have performed high-pressure water jet cleaning, and this is obviously helped a lot in removing this bitumen layer and increasing the grip level for the test that we had with F3, we expect the track to be in slightly worse condition because in the next weeks.

"Some dust will come down, and the grip level will reduce a little bit. But we expect to start the week in a very good condition in this sense. In terms of the circuit itself, obviously the turn with the banking is the most critical and most severe; it is probably the most severe turn in the championship.

"We need to gather the real data, let's say, but on paper and from simulations, it seems so because it's a very long turn, limited by grip, not by the power, so they will be on the limit.

"Zandvoort is not grip limited now; it's power limited, and also in terms of duration, it is less in terms of seconds.

"I guess that if we see the pure energy that the turn gives to the tyres, it's higher. We are speaking about 20-20 per cent higher energy compared to the reference of Zandvoort.

"They can also try to they can try different approaches to that turn, different race lines, so it's very demanding that turn. For the rest, the walls are pretty close. We had a lot of red flags during the test, and with a lot of interruptions, that could be another factor.

"It's considered a normal street circuit like Singapore, so I would not be surprised to have significant incidents, let's say, or interruptions during both practice and the race."

title: McLaren eye F1 victory return with three tracks highlighted
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has named three F1 tracks at which McLaren could once again impose itself in the fight for victory.

The Woking-based squad was unable to be a significant factor at Monza last weekend, with Mercedes possessing the fastest package.

Kimi Antonelli and George Russell brought home a 1-2 finish, with the former winning after starting from 19th on the grid.

Lando Norris ended the race in fourth place after making a last-lap overtake on team-mate Oscar Piastri, but it was a largely mellow weekend for the team that won the two races prior to Monza.

However, Stella does not see McLaren's chances of success now over, insisting upcoming tracks will play into its hands.

“A good, sensible, realistic end of the year is an end of the year in which the final nine or 10 races, we will see are sessions in which we can be consistently fighting for victories and achieve some of these victories,” he said.

“I think our tracks will be more the likes of Malaysia, Austin, Brazil. Here we have some long corners that seem to express its potential well.

“We have some new upgrades that we will take to Baku, but we still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.”

However, Stella is expecting the car to be more competitive this weekend in Madrid compared to Monza.

“Yet we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary, we were in position to win races, and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race,” he said.

“This drag will be less important in Madrid, there's a much higher density of corners. So we will definitely give it a go.

“But from a championship point of view, I think we have to remain very realistic, don't get conditioned by looking at the classification. Just focus on one race at a time.”

title: Kimi Antonelli historic Italian GP victory rated - by the driver who won from further back
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli's victory in the Italian Grand Prix was the first time a driver had won from 19th on the grid since the 1954 Indianapolis 500 - some 1,128 world championship races ago.

But remarkably, Antonelli and Bill Vukovich have been one-upped by one driver who won from 22nd on the grid.

That was John Watson in the 1983 United States West GP at Long Beach as he stormed from 22nd on the 23-car grid to enter the record books and assume a record, which, having stood for 44 years and 787 grands prix, is likely to stand the test of time.

Reflecting on Antonelli's incredible drive, his seventh win of the season, and one which opened up a 66-point lead in the drivers' championship over George Russell, Watson has evaluated the Italian's achievement - and labelled him as a "fundamentally racer" who possesses a "unique" ability.

"There are some drivers who are what I would call fundamentally racers, and the people mentioned [above] were people that I would describe as racers,” Watson told Motor Sport.

"There are many fine racing drivers who have won grands prix and have been world champions, who have not, in my view, been what I would describe as an out-and-out racer.”

"It’s having this ability to make judgments when you’re catching a car. You must catch it in the right part of the racetrack to enable you to continue that progress, not to find yourself being bogged down and then losing your momentum.

"It comes down to a variety of qualities in the personality of the person and their ability behind the wheel to make those assessments and judgments. Execution is key ultimately, and you’ve got to be decisive.

"What he is doing presently is remarkable. George Russell, I’ve got a great respect for. I think he’s a bloody quick guy, and Kimi’s really overshadowing him, totally.

"Everybody felt it was George’s race to lose, and as it turns out, he did, and it was to his own team-mate.

"Antonelli has got something which is currently, I would say, unique amongst the entire Formula 1 field: a kid who’s just turned 20 with that maturity, along with that ability.

"It was a stellar drive, a world champion’s drive, and something that I think that he will be satisfied with, and quite rightly so as well."

title: Lewis Hamilton left stunned by 'mind-blowing' F1 rival advantage
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has stated Mercedes' straight-line advantage was “mind-blowing” during the Italian Grand Prix.

Hamilton endured a challenging weekend at Monza, having entered the event hoping to give the Tifosi the chance to see a Ferrari on the top step of the podium.

The seven-time champion was shuffled down the order on the opening lap after going wheel-to-wheel with team-mate Charles Leclerc at the first corner.

Forced into a recovery drive, Hamilton could only climb to sixth place - matching his lowest result of the season.

While Hamilton was content with his car through the corners, he conceded it was unable to keep up when it came to the straights.

“I was in the fight, doing good, the grip felt good, and the car felt generally decent through the corners,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“Just on the straight, we knew that they [Mercedes] were fast on the straight.

“But it was really mind-blowing just how quick they were in the straight with Mercedes power.

“That thing just keeps pulling, pulling, pulling.”

Mercedes won Sunday's race, with Kimi Antonelli rising from 19th on the grid to first place.

While Antonelli displayed strong pace in the early stages to rise through the field, a stop under a virtual safety car further aided his route to victory - but Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur insisted such a stop was not possible for Hamilton.

"The pace was huge,” Vasseur said. "And on top of this, he also had the capacity to stop because he had the top speed to overtake and to come back.

“A good example is the last VSC. I think we had the same gap with Max before and after the VSC.

"But in our case, if you pit, you are behind Tunoda and Gasly and I'm not sure that you were able to overtake them.

“On top of this, when you have this kind of deficit, you are taking risks. You have to take options on the strategy, not always make it work.

title: Charles Leclerc shares personal update after major Monza crash
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has taken to social media to detail that he feels “okay” after his heavy crash at the Italian Grand Prix.

Leclerc was battling Oscar Piastri in the early stages of the race when he lost control of his Ferrari car at the final corner.

The Monegasque suffered a heavy crash into the barrier, however he was able to walk away from the wreckage on his own feet.

Leclerc told media including RacingNews365, after his assessment by the trackside doctor, that he suffered vision issues in the first minutes after the crash.

With the Spanish Grand Prix taking place so soon after the Monza event, Leclerc detailed that he would have to undergo further tests to ensure he was fit enough to compete in Madrid.

Speaking on social media, Leclerc hinted that he is fit for the weekend, stating: “Not how I wanted the weekend to go.

“Thanks for all the messages. Physically, that was a big one, but I’m okay.

“Emotionally, it hurts even more for something like this to happen here at home, in front of all of you, the tifosi.

Leclerc enters the upcoming Madrid weekend fifth in the drivers' standings.

title: Liam Lawson delivers 'not ideal' verdict after Monza frustration
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has stated it was “not ideal” to take an engine-related grid penalty at the Italian Grand Prix.

The New Zealander continued his substitute stint at Red Bull last weekend as Isack Hadjar recovers from a wrist injury picked up during the summer break.

Red Bull used the weekend to introduce a new engine to Hadjar's pool, with Lawson taking the grid penalty hit.

It meant that he had to start the race from the back of the grid as he looked to add to his points tally this year.

“We’ve taken the engine penalty, so we really focused on long runs [during practice],” Lawson told media including RacingNews365.

“Obviously, it's not great, not ideal taking an engine. But I think we had the speed to come through.

“We’d done all the work to have a good race car, which we did. It's just unfortunate we had some issues yesterday, which we were able to resolve today for the race, and the car was much better.

Lawson ended the race in 14th place, marking just the fourth time this year that he has failed to cross the line inside the top 10.

His task was made more difficult when several midfield runners pitted under a virtual safety, giving them a fresh tyre boost.

When asked what would have been possible without the VSC intervention, Lawson said: “We were quick enough to come right through, so probably more points.”

title: Franco Colapinto hands Alpine apology after Max Verstappen fight
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has apologised to his Alpine team for his mistake on the Italian Grand Prix restart, following his "cool" fight with Max Verstappen.

The Argentine driver restarted fourth following the red flag for Charles Leclerc's early crash, and was side-by-side with Verstappen through Curva Grande on the opening lap of the second phase of the race, before the Red Bull nipped ahead into the second chicane.

Colapinto then found himself battling Lewis Hamilton in fourth place around the first Lesmo corner, but in mid-corner, he had a snap of oversteer, which when corrected, spat the Alpine off into the gravel and well down the order.

Colapinto eventually recovered to take ninth place and earn two points, his first since 10th in Belgium, as pole-sitting team-mate Pierre Gasly took seventh.

However, reflecting, Colapinto was apologetic to his team for potentially costing it more points.

"I think when you're in the car, you don't really kind of feel the difference if it's one driver or another, but it was cool to be fighting with them," Colapinto said of his restart battle with Verstappen to media, including RacingNews365.

"To be fighting side by side with the top cars and the top teams, we cannot really do it, and so to just miss an opportunity like this, it's very painful.

"The big three, it's very good. I was with four of the top teams' cars on the restart, and that's why it hurts so much to throw it away. By taking more risks and being up there with them, you don't realise that it's not really your fight. You feel in the moment, and you want to give your all. I'm taking risks, and maybe it makes sense.

"I just lost the car completely in Turn Six, a bit out of nowhere. Fighting with the top teams gets you very motivated very quickly.

"I will learn for the future. We don't get many of these opportunities fighting up there at the front, and it's extra frustrating to have moments like this. I think we should have scored more points, so I'm sorry for the team."

title: Lewis Hamilton told to 'accept the consequences' of Charles Leclerc attack
excerpt:
Former F1 driver David Coulthard has stated Lewis Hamilton must “accept the consequences” for his approach to racing Charles Leclerc at the Italian Grand Prix.

Hamilton attacked Leclerc into the first corner of the race but was subsequently pushed into the gravel on the corner exit.

It caused the seven-time champion to drop down the order, forcing him into a recovery drive at the team's home race.

Coulthard noted that Leclerc was more than fair to Hamilton through the opening corner and was entitled to run him out of road on the exit.

“I thought Lewis was brilliant on the brakes, and I thought Charles was very fair in giving him the space,” Coulthard told the Up To Speed podcast.

“Charles has had the presence of his position to give the space to Lewis on the inside, but he's got the absolute right to run on the outside, which then becomes the inside for the next corner.

“Yes, he's taken the racing line, which forces Lewis off, but Lewis has a choice.

“When you put yourself on the outside, you're at the mercy of the car on the inside. So it's a higher risk than if you're on the inside.

“He put himself at the mercy of the car on the inside. His team-mate said, 'No, I'm not giving you room now. I've given you room on the way into Turn 1.

“On the way through Turn 2, you've got a choice: you stay there, or you go to the gravel. He made his choice, and he was put to the gravel.”

Hamilton voiced his frustration over team radio and later called on Ferrari to implement ground rules going forward.

However, Coulthard suggested Hamilton should have been anticipating such a move from Leclerc.

“I can understand absolutely why Lewis would not be happy with that because I wouldn't be happy and you wouldn't be happy,” he said.

“But if you put yourself in that position, you have to accept the consequences as well, and the fact that the stewards didn't apply any penalty would suggest that they just called it a racing incident.”

title: Michael Schumacher contract saga erupts at Monza after rival swoop
excerpt:
Michael Schumacher drove one race for Jordan in 1991, and the entire battle for his signature ultimately came down to a single word.

In the letter of intent the German signed before his debut at Spa-Francorchamps, his management had secretly changed “the contract” to “a contract.”

It was a small difference on paper, a big difference in practice. Schumacher thereby promised to sign a contract at some point, but not necessarily a racing contract with Jordan Grand Prix.

From a sporting perspective, that single race was already more than just a showcase.

Schumacher qualified impressively in seventh place but came to a stop in the race due to clutch problems. Still, that one lap was fast enough to shake up the paddock.

Benetton team boss Flavio Briatore saw his chance, pounced on it immediately after that weekend, and skillfully exploited the loophole in the preliminary agreement.

This was possible because, in 1991, F1 had no authority whatsoever to monitor dual driver contracts. Whoever had the smartest lawyer, the fattest wallet, or simply the most influence in the paddock came out on top.

Eddie Jordan went to an Italian court to block the move, but was rebuffed: a letter of intent with such a loosely worded clause was no match for a team that put a real contract on the table.

The decision wasn’t made in a courtroom, but in the Monza paddock, with Bernie Ecclestone mediating between Briatore and Jordan. The matter was settled through a game of musical chairs, not by a judge.

Domino effect at Monza

There was a problem for Benetton, however, as it didn’t have an open seat. To make room for Schumacher, Briatore sidelined Roberto Moreno - the very man who had finished fourth at Spa.

Moreno was not amused and threatened to take the matter to court himself. He was bought off with a sum that, according to insiders, ranged from five to nearly six hundred thousand dollars, and then moved on to the seat Schumacher had vacated at Jordan. Exactly what was agreed upon between Benetton, Jordan, and Moreno never fully came to light.

Thus, Jordan got an experienced driver as a consolation prize, Moreno got money and a seat, and Benetton simply got the greatest talent of his generation. Only the debt Eddie Jordan had outstanding with Schumacher himself remained unpaid.

That matter wasn’t fully settled until April 1997, when Schumacher reportedly transferred about one million dollars. By then, Jordan had long since ceased to be an underdog or a rookie, and Schumacher had become a two-time world champion.

Jordan never minced words about how heated emotions ran at the time: he acknowledged the friction and the annoyance, and that he had taken the matter to an Italian court.

Briatore described it as a battle on multiple fronts at once, with Jordan on one side and Tom Walkinshaw representing Benetton on the other. Both team bosses were later able to laugh it off, which is of course easier when you were on the winning side.

The aftershocks of this whole affair are greater than the anecdotal story itself. The chaos surrounding Schumacher and Moreno was, in fact, the direct catalyst for the establishment of the FIA Contract Recognition Board in 1992.

Since then, every F1 driver’s contract must be registered in Geneva, where the CRB decides which contract takes precedence. As a result, lengthy legal disputes between teams have largely disappeared from the sport; FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem still referred to it in the conflict surrounding Oscar Piastri in 2022 as the mechanism for resolving this kind of issue.

There’s also another side to this story. Even with a CRB in place, Schumacher likely wouldn’t have stayed long with a team that was fifth in the constructors’ championship at the time, with 13 points compared to Benetton’s 33.

The main difference lies in the speed: without that loophole in the letter of intent, the move would have taken months or even an entire season, rather than just one weekend.

For Jordan, it remained a bitter pill to swallow that his team had discovered the talent, let him make his debut, and ultimately gained nothing from it except a recently fired driver and, six years later, a settlement.
